how-much-to-charge-for-duct-cleaning.htm.text:
← Duct cleaning bid calculator

How much to charge for duct cleaning

Independent HVAC and duct-cleaning shops get shopped on a published $99 whole-house special. That price cannot see the job. One furnace and ten vents on a ranch is not the same work as a two-system colonial with extra returns, a crawl, and a coil clean. Matching the coupon is how a sold colonial becomes a loss after the first extra air handler.

Price the systems and the vents, not “a house”

A typical advertised special includes one system, about ten supply vents, one return, and one story. Everything past that is extra labor: another air handler, more boots, a second story of ladder time, crawl or tight-attic access, moving furniture in an occupied house, pulling an evaporator coil, fogging sanitizer, or fighting pet hair. Those lines do not scale with “whole house.”

The free duct cleaning bid calculator starts from that included ranch, then bills extra systems, extra vents, extra returns, extra stories, crawl access, occupancy, coil clean, sanitizer, and heavy debris as their own hours. You get the bid, the price per vent, and the walk-away number below which the job makes nothing.

What a $99 special actually covers

On a one-system, ten-vent, one-story ranch with no coil and no crawl, a shop that loads a $32 wage at 28% burden, adds a filter and truck time, then keeps 28% margin lands near $323, with a walk-away around $233. A $99 coupon is already underwater on that ranch. A $299 “after-coupon” price still covers the ranch. The same $299 on a two-system, 18-vent colonial with crawl, occupancy, coil, and sanitizer is below walk-away — that house prices near $800.

Those figures are ballpark starting points from editable hours, not a recommended price. Replace every rate with a takeoff from your own crew.

What this is not

This is not HVAC maintenance (filters and tune-ups), dryer-vent cleaning, restaurant hood / NFPA-96 work, a chimney sweep, or a mini-split install. It is not a NADCA certification, an indoor-air-quality test, a mold finding, a warranty, or legal, tax, or financial advice. Confirm system count, vent count, access, and every number before you send a bid.

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying the output before relying on it.

Common questions

How much to charge for duct cleaning?

Charge from the systems, the supply vents, the stories, and the extras — not from a published $99 whole-house special. A one-system ranch with ten vents and no coil clean is a different job from a two-system colonial with extra returns, crawl access, and an evaporator-coil clean. Price each of those lines, then add loaded labor, filters, truck time, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep.

Why does a $99 duct cleaning special lose money?

The coupon is written for one furnace and a handful of vents on a ranch. Extra air handlers, extra vents, a second story, crawl or tight-attic access, an occupied home, a coil clean, sanitizer, and heavy pet hair do not come with that price. Matching the coupon on a two-system house is how a sold job becomes a loss after the first extra system.

Is this a NADCA price or an indoor-air-quality test?

No. The numbers are arithmetic on the shop's own hours and costs. They are not a NADCA certification, a mold finding, an indoor-air-quality test, a warranty, or a recommended price.

      Common questions

      What does this duct cleaning estimate include?

      The price adds up loaded labor for the base setup plus every extra system, vent, return, and story beyond the ones you mark as included, plus crawl access, occupied-home protection, a coil clean, sanitizer, and heavy debris — then filters per system, consumables, sanitizer cost, travel and equipment, overhead, and your target margin. Nothing is a flat “$99 whole-house special” regardless of how many systems or vents the house actually has.

      Why do systems, vents, returns, and stories only bill past what's “included”?

      Every job type already assumes a base setup — the one-system, 10-vent ranch the presets call the $99/$299 special — so the “included” fields are what that base setup already covers. Only systems, vents, returns, and stories beyond those thresholds add hours, which is why a two-system colonial with 18 vents and a crawl prices well above the ranch special even though both start from the same base setup hours.

      Why do coil clean, sanitizer, and heavy debris each get a separate checkbox instead of one lump “deep clean” option?

      Each is a distinct task with its own hours and, for sanitizer, its own material cost — an evaporator coil clean, an antimicrobial fog, and extra time for pet hair or construction debris don't always travel together. Pricing them separately means a job with heavy debris but no coil work isn't charged for a coil clean it doesn't need, and vice versa.

      Why does crawl access add hours but occupied-home doesn't add a material cost?

      Crawl or tight-attic access is purely a labor problem — it takes longer to reach and rig equipment in a confined space, with no extra materials. Occupied-home is the same: extra care and cleanup working around a resident adds hours but no separate line on the parts side. Coil and sanitizer, by contrast, use materials (a coil cleaner, an antimicrobial fog) on top of the hours.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. A share link encodes only the inputs you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your vent count, wages, costs, or prices. Only your business name and contact details for the printed proposal are kept in this browser's local storage, and “Forget my business details” clears them.

      Does this check indoor air quality, mold, or duct integrity?

      No. Hours and material costs are ballpark shop figures you can edit, not an indoor-air-quality test, a mold finding, a NADCA certification, a warranty, or a guarantee that any system will pass a later inspection. Cleaning removes accumulated debris from the existing ductwork; whether the ducts themselves are sealed, sized, or in good repair is a separate judgment call for the site visit.

vs-a-flat-whole-house-special.html.text:
← Duct Cleaning Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat whole-house duct-cleaning special

"$99 whole-house" or "$299 after coupon" is not a price for a duct-cleaning job — it is a price for one system and ten vents, quietly applied to a two-system split-level with crawl access and a coil clean.

What a flat whole-house special is

A flat whole-house price is the fastest way to quote off a coupon page or a truck wrap: one number next to "duct cleaning near me." Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between companies, and it is the number a caller holding a competitor's coupon will ask you to match on their own house.

The number behind it was set for one job — usually a single system with about ten supply vents on one story, unoccupied, no coil clean, no sanitizer — and then reused for every house afterward, whether or not the next one has a second air handler, extra vents, crawl access, a family still living there, or a coil that needs cleaning too.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the job type, the number of systems, supply vents, returns, and stories, and whether the job needs crawl access, is occupied, needs a coil clean, sanitizer, or has heavy debris, along with your own wage, payroll burden, travel, and overhead. It prices the extra system, the extra vents and returns, the extra story, and each add-on separately, and returns a walk-away price and price per vent below which the job loses money — for this house, not a generic one.

Job$299 after-coupon specialWalk-away priceVerdict
1-system ranch, 10 vents, 1 story (this calculator's own default job)$299.00$232.91Covers, $66.09 to spare
1-system 14-vent ranch, occupied, coil clean + sanitizer$299.00$362.12Short $63.12
2-system colonial, 18 vents, crawl access, occupied, coil clean + sanitizer$299.00$600.50Short $301.50

Worked using this calculator's own job presets at a $32 hourly wage, 28% payroll burden, 16% overhead on direct cost, and a 28% target margin — the form's own shipped defaults, not numbers invented for this page. Open the calculator to check any row yourself.

Notice the top row: it is this calculator's own shipped starting point, not a job picked to prove a point, and a $299 after-coupon special already clears it by less than seventy dollars. One occupied home, one coil clean, or one extra system is the difference between a special that happens to work and one that does not.

What a flat whole-house special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same price whether the house has one air handler or two — a second system adds its own setup, not a share of the first. Adds hours per system beyond the first included in the base setup, so a two-system house prices differently from a one-system one.
Has no separate line for vent count above the advertised ten, or for returns, so a 22-vent split-level gets the same price as a 10-vent ranch. Adds hours per extra supply vent and per extra return beyond the presets included in the special, scaled to the count entered.
Prices "a house" the same whether it is one story or two, and whether the crew needs crawl access to reach the trunk line. Adds hours per extra story and for crawl access separately, only when the job needs them.
Has no line for working around a family still living in the house, for cleaning the evaporator coil, for sanitizer, or for heavy pet-hair debris. Prices occupied-home time, a coil clean, sanitizer, and heavy debris as their own hours, each added only when selected.
Gives the technician a price to quote, not a number to check a quote against when a caller's house turns out to be a two-system split-level with crawl access after the special was already promised. Reports the walk-away price and price per vent for the job as entered, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before it is confirmed.

A flat whole-house special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied to a system count, vent count, story count, or access condition it was not set on, and "a house" alone never tells you that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat special skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat whole-house duct-cleaning special get the price wrong?

Because duct-cleaning cost scales with the number of systems, supply vents, returns, stories, crawl access, occupancy, a coil clean, sanitizer, and heavy debris — not with "a house." A one-system ranch with ten vents is a different job from a two-system split-level with extra vents, crawl access, an occupied home, and a coil clean. A flat house price quotes both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat whole-house special usually leave out entirely?

The extra system, the extra vents and returns, the extra story, crawl access, occupancy, the coil clean, and sanitizer. A published whole-house price is set on one configuration — usually a single system with about ten vents on one story, unoccupied, no coil, no sanitizer — and has no separate line for a second air handler, a crawl-space run, working around a family still living there, cleaning the evaporator coil, or a heavy pet-hair job.

How much do extra systems, vents, stories, and access actually add over the special?

On this calculator's own worked examples, at a $32 hourly wage, 28% burden, 16% overhead, and a 28% target margin: this calculator's own shipped one-system, ten-vent, one-story default — the form's starting point, not a job picked to make a point — walks away at $232.91, comfortably under a $299 after-coupon special. A one-system, 14-vent ranch with an occupied home, a coil clean, and sanitizer walks away at $362.12, $63.12 short of that same $299. A two-system colonial with 18 vents, crawl access, an occupied home, a coil clean, and sanitizer walks away at $600.50, $301.50 short. A two-system, 22-vent split-level with crawl access, heavy pet hair, and a coil clean walks away at $679.99, $380.99 short of the same $299 special.

Is a flat whole-house special ever the right way to quote?

For something close to the easy job it was probably priced on — one system, about ten vents, one story, unoccupied, no coil or sanitizer add-on — a flat rate can land close, and on this calculator's own numbers even the default job only clears it by $66.09. The risk is a second system, extra vents or returns, an extra story, crawl access, an occupied home, a coil clean, sanitizer, or heavy debris stacking on top of each other, because a flat house price has no way to see any of them until the crew is already on site.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates or what competitors charge. It takes the systems, vents, returns, stories, crawl access, occupancy, coil clean, sanitizer, and heavy debris you enter, plus your own wage, burden, and overhead, and turns them into a walk-away price for the job you describe — the arithmetic a flat special skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat whole-house special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the system, vent, and access count it was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is account-based field-service software for running a home-service business across clients, scheduling, and crews. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this duct-cleaning job cost, given its systems and access, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one duct-cleaning job's type (residential, two-system, heavy-debris, or light-commercial), extra air handlers, extra supply vents, extra returns, extra stories, crawl access, an occupied home, an evaporator-coil clean, sanitizer, and heavy debris, plus loaded wage, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the price per vent, the hours the first extra system actually consumes, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
